title: Can AI Accurately Estimate Nutrition From a Food Photo?

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> AI is entering oncology workflows faster than evidence on stakeholder acceptance, trust, and sustained use. Existing syntheses rarely distinguish anticipated attitudes from actual use across oncology stakeholders. <strong>Objective:</strong> The aim of the study is to synthesize primary empirical evidence on stakeholder acceptance, trust, and implementation of AI in oncology and examine variation by stakeholder group, clinical task, AI exposure, and implementation maturity. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a Joanna Briggs Institute–guided mixed methods systematic review with convergent integrated synthesis; the protocol was registered before formal eligibility screening. Eight databases were searched without date or language limits (August 6-9, 2026), yielding 46,206 records and 31,802 unique records. Title and abstract screening used 2 balanced primary allocations, joint bidirectional readjudication, and blinded verification of a stratified 10% (n=3182) sample. Full-text assessment, extraction, and critical appraisal were dual independent. Acceptance/Trust modes and F1-F8 coverage were independently coded across 309 studies and reconciled. Eight integrated findings were anchored to the nonadoption, abandonment, scale-up, spread, and sustainability framework; an emergent economic finding was reported separately. Adjusted stage models controlled for study design, publication format, and publication period; robustness analyses examined screening provenance and appraisal sensitivity. <strong>Results:</strong> We included 309 primary empirical studies; 187 (60.5%) were published in 2025 or 2026. Exposure ranged from hypothetical opinion to real-world implementation (n=82 studies), but only 6 described routine use. Acceptance was empirically assessed in 267 studies and Trust in 127. Relative to anticipatory stage 1, Acceptance assessment was less frequent in evaluated-interaction stage 2 (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] 0.07, 95% CI 0.02-0.25; <i>P</i><.001) and stages 3+4 (aOR 0.12, 95% CI 0.03-0.45; <i>P</i>=.001). Transparency/explainability coverage (F3) was lower in stages 3+4 (aOR 0.20, 95% CI 0.08-0.47; <i>q</i><0.001). Workflow/interoperability coverage (F5) was higher and governance coverage (F7) lower in both later contrasts after false discovery rate correction. Trust declined descriptively across stages, but adjusted contrasts were nonsignificant. Eight integrated findings spanned clinical value, performance, transparency, oversight, workflow, readiness, governance, and implementation, plus an emergent stage 1 economic finding. The principal Acceptance, F3, F5, and F7 findings persisted in the 229-study original screening subset. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> In oncology, the AI evidence profile appears to differ from anticipated use to implementation. Acceptance was empirically assessed most often before deployment; later-stage studies more often examined workflow and less often examined transparency and governance. The challenge is whether favorable attitudes and early deployment translate into calibrated, governed, and sustained routine use. An interpretive stage-specific model identifies assessment priorities across exposure and implementation contexts, but is not a validated causal or predictive model. Later-stage evaluations should retain measurement of Acceptance, trust calibration, governance, durability, and workflow outcomes. <strong>Trial Registration:</strong> OSF Registries osf.io/nmep8; https://osf.io/nmep8
title: Stakeholder Acceptance, Trust, and Implementation of AI in Oncology: Mixed Methods Systematic Review

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> The rise of online data collection in psychological and health research has been accompanied by an increase in fraudulent participation, threatening data quality and research integrity. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aimed to examine how fraud manifests across different research contexts, evaluate the detection methods used, and develop practical recommendations for a range of remote research settings. <strong>Methods:</strong> This exploratory qualitative study was conducted with six UK-based research teams (n=12 individuals) who had encountered fraudulent participants in their remote studies (January 2009-January 2026). Teams were purposively selected to represent diversity across target population (children, adolescents, and adults), study methodology (online surveys, ecological momentary assessment, qualitative interviews, and online diaries), recruitment approach, and research topic (mental health, loneliness, healthy aging, alcohol consumption, and genetic cohort building). Data were collected between June and September 2025 using semistructured interviews and open-ended questionnaires and analyzed using reflexive thematic analysis within a broadly realist framework. <strong>Results:</strong> Teams described fraud as context dependent, manifesting differently according to study design, recruitment method, and target population. Key themes pertained to how fraud is recognized, the contextual factors that shape its presentation, vulnerability factors (eg, social media recruitment and financial compensation), the challenges and limitations of detection methods, the burden on researchers’ time and resources, and gaps in institutional preparedness. Detection approaches ranged from systematic methods, such as IP address inspection and demographic consistency checks, to more interpretive strategies, such as what teams describe as “interviewer intuition” in qualitative studies. Teams reported adapting their prevention strategies iteratively through experience. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> The findings of this study suggest that one-size-fits-all solutions are inadequate and that fraud detection and prevention approaches need to be tailored to study design, recruitment methods, and resource constraints. We recommend that fraud mitigation planning be considered a standard requirement in research funding applications.
title: Detection and Mitigation of Fraudulent Participants in Online Psychology and Health Research: Exploratory Qualitative Study of Researcher Experiences

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Adverse childhood experiences (ACEs) are associated with poorer adult health, but the behavioral and informational pathways underlying these associations, and whether digital environments condition them, remain unclear. Clarifying whether these pathways vary across contemporary digital contexts may help explain heterogeneity in the long-term health correlates of early adversity. <strong>Objective:</strong> Guided by the life course perspective, this study examined whether ACE exposure was indirectly associated with adverse adult health through tobacco and alcohol use risk (TAUR) and health literacy (HL), and whether social media use (SMU) moderated these pathways. <strong>Methods:</strong> We analyzed data from 30,054 adults in the 2023 Psychology and Behavior Investigation of Chinese Residents. A moderated dual-mediation structural equation model specified TAUR and HL as parallel mediators and SMU as a first-stage moderator. Robust maximum likelihood estimation was used. Conditional indirect associations at the SMU mean and at ±1 SD were estimated using 100,000-draw Monte Carlo 95% CIs. <strong>Results:</strong> Greater ACE exposure was associated with higher TAUR (B=0.118, 95% CI 0.101-0.135; <i>P</i><.001) and lower HL (B=–0.028, 95% CI –0.036 to –0.020; <i>P</i><.001). At mean SMU, indirect associations were positive through TAUR (B=0.020, 95% CI 0.014-0.027; <i>P</i><.001) and HL (B=0.004, 95% CI 0.003-0.006; <i>P</i><.001). For TAUR, the ACE association was smaller at higher levels of SMU (interaction B=–0.034, 95% CI –0.042 to –0.025; <i>P</i><.001). The conditional indirect association was B=0.026 at low SMU and B=0.015 at high SMU, with an index of moderated mediation of –0.006 (95% CI –0.008 to –0.004; <i>P</i><.001). For HL, the interaction was also negative (B=–0.043, 95% CI –0.051 to –0.035; <i>P</i><.001), and the indirect association through HL was negative at low SMU (B=–0.002, 95% CI –0.004 to –0.001; <i>P</i>=.002) but positive at high SMU (B=0.011, 95% CI 0.008-0.013; <i>P</i><.001), with an index of moderated mediation of 0.006 (95% CI 0.005-0.008; <i>P</i><.001). Johnson-Neyman analyses showed that the ACE to TAUR association remained statistically significant across the observed SMU range, whereas the ACE to HL association was positive below –0.855 SD, nonsignificant between –0.855 and –0.472 SD, and negative above –0.472 SD. The conditional indirect associations were statistically significant but small in magnitude. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> ACE exposure was associated with adult health through distinct behavioral and informational pathways that varied across SMU levels. These findings may inform the development and evaluation of interventions addressing TAUR and health information use in social media–rich environments.
title: Social Media Use as a Moderator of Behavioral and Health Literacy Pathways Between Adverse Childhood Experiences and Adult Health: Nationwide Cross-Sectional Study

summary: Background: AI is increasingly applied across health care domains, yet public trust in AI across racial and ethnic groups and across health domains is poorly understood. Objective: This study examined trust in AI relative to trust in human professionals and identified sociodemographic characteristics associated with this comparative trust. Methods: A cross-sectional survey was conducted among 10,506 US adults from the Understanding America Study (UAS), a probability-based internet panel, with poststratification survey weights applied to descriptive estimates to characterize the US adult population. Data were analyzed using multinomial logistic regression, adjusted for the sociodemographic characteristics used in poststratification survey weights. Trust in AI relative to human professionals was assessed for mental health counseling (the primary outcome), health diagnoses, and diet and exercise planning. Responses were categorized as “less trust than in a human professional,” “the same level of trust as in a human professional” (parity trust), “more trust than in a human professional” (superiority trust), or “not sure.” Results: Among the 10,506 participants (n=6385, 51.3% [percentage weighted using poststratification survey weights] female; mean age 49.3, SD 17.0 years), most trusted AI less than they trusted human professionals for health diagnosis and mental health counseling. Trust was lowest for mental health counseling (1136/10,469, 11.9% reported parity or superiority trust) and highest for diet and exercise planning (4773/10,460, 43.2%). For mental health counseling, non-Hispanic (NH) Black, Hispanic, and NH Asian adults were more likely than NH White adults to endorse parity trust, and these groups and NH multiracial adults were more likely to endorse superiority trust. NH Asian adults were 2.5 times more likely to endorse parity trust (relative risk ratio [RRR] 2.58, 95% CI 2.04-3.25; <i>P</i><.001) and nearly 6 times more likely to endorse superiority trust (RRR 5.95, 95% CI 3.79-9.35; <i>P</i><.001) for mental health counseling. NH Black (RRR 3.32, 95% CI 2.19-5.05; <i>P</i><.001), Hispanic (RRR 2.41, 95% CI 1.60-3.65; <i>P</i><.001), and NH multiracial (RRR 3.57, 95% CI 2.06-6.19; <i>P</i><.001) adults also showed elevated superiority trust. For mental health counseling, all racial and ethnic minority groups were more likely than NH White adults to select “not sure.” Generative AI use for general purposes was associated with higher trust, whereas higher education levels were associated with lower trust. Conclusions: NH Black, Hispanic, NH Asian, and NH multiracial adults were more likely than NH White adults to trust AI more than human professionals for mental health counseling. These data cannot show whether higher trust leads to greater use, and higher trust should not be interpreted as a preference for AI over human-delivered care. Nonetheless, this pattern informs how mental health AI tools can be designed, evaluated, and governed, as individuals with the greatest trust in these tools may be most affected if the tools perform poorly.
title: Racial and Ethnic Differences in Trust in AI Relative to Human Professionals for Health Care: Nationally Representative Cross-Sectional Study

summary: <strong>Background:</strong> Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly applied in clinical text processing, but their role in emergency departments (EDs) and ED-adjacent emergency care remains unclear because ED electronic health records (EHRs) are heterogeneous, time-critical, and safety-sensitive. <strong>Objective:</strong> This study aims to synthesize peer-reviewed evidence on LLM applications to real-world ED EHR data and ED-adjacent emergency care data, focusing on clinical tasks, technical strategies, evaluation practices, and workflow integration. <strong>Methods:</strong> We conducted a PRISMA (Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses)–guided systematic review of PubMed and Web of Science (January 1, 2022, to November 14, 2025). We included peer-reviewed English-language studies applying LLM strategies to ED and ED-adjacent EHR data. We extracted dataset characteristics, model families, task formulations (classification, summarization, and information extraction), adaptation strategies (prompting, fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, and agentic/hybrid workflows), evaluation metrics, and ED workflow phase. Two reviewers also independently completed a design-matched methodological quality and risk-of-bias appraisal. <strong>Results:</strong> Thirty-one studies met our inclusion criteria. Many relied on single-center datasets (n=12), relatively small sample sizes (<10,000 encounters; n=20), and English-language unstructured text alone or mixed EHR inputs combining text with structured or semistructured fields. Prompt engineering was the dominant adaptation strategy (n=27), while fine-tuning, retrieval-augmented generation, and hybrid/agentic pipelines were less common. Postencounter studies frequently demonstrated task-specific retrospective technical feasibility, while triage, diagnostic-support, and disposition studies evaluated heterogeneous tasks and outcomes; these nonequivalent measures were not compared as indicators of workflow maturity. Workflow-phase assignment did not imply real-time integration, particularly when model inputs were available only after the relevant clinical decision point. Overall, 22 (71%) studies were classified as technical-performance-only evaluations; clinical utility was empirically assessed in only 3 (9.7%) studies, and prospective deployment in 4 (12.9%). No study directly measured patient outcomes or downstream patient-safety outcomes attributable to LLM use. <strong>Conclusions:</strong> Current LLM applications across ED and ED-adjacent emergency care primarily function as documentation, surveillance, and auditing assistants rather than autonomous decision engines. Progress toward safe, deployable systems will require larger multicenter datasets, external and prospective validation, safety- and fairness-centered evaluation, and governance mechanisms that support responsible clinical integration. However, most evidence remains technical or retrospective, while prospective workflow integration, empirically demonstrated clinical utility, patient safety, and patient benefit remain insufficiently evaluated.
title: Large Language Models for Electronic Health Records in Emergency Department (ED) and ED-Adjacent Emergency Care—Technical Strategies, Clinical Tasks, and Workflow Integration: Systematic Review

summary: Background: Sarcopenia is an age-related syndrome characterized by muscle loss and functional decline, increasing fall risks. Early identification is crucial, yet convenient and accurate screening tools remain limited in routine practice. Machine learning (ML) models show promise for early sarcopenia detection, but their diagnostic performance and methodological quality have not been systematically quantified. Objective: This review aimed to quantitatively evaluate the diagnostic performance of ML models for sarcopenia prediction, compare performance across ML algorithms, and identify key sources of heterogeneity and methodological limitations. Methods: PubMed, Web of Science, Embase, and the Cochrane Library were systematically searched from inception to April 15, 2026. Eligible studies developed or validated at least one ML model for sarcopenia and provided sufficient data to reconstruct a 2×2 contingency table. Risk of bias was assessed using PROBAST (Prediction Model Risk of Bias Assessment Tool) developed by Moons et al. The primary analysis used a bivariate random‑effects (Reitsma) model to jointly synthesize sensitivity and specificity. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) values were pooled using a univariate random‑effects model with the Hartung‑Knapp‑Sidik‑Jonkman (HKSJ) method, and 95% prediction intervals (PIs) were estimated. A secondary analysis incorporated all models using cluster-robust variance estimation (RVE). Subgroup analyses and meta‑regression explored heterogeneity. The certainty of evidence was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE). Results: Twenty studies (20 prespecified index models) were included. The pooled AUROC was 0.89 (95% CI 0.82-0.93; 95% PI 0.54-0.98), with pooled sensitivity of 0.77 (95% CI 0.68-0.83; 95% PI 0.37-0.95) and specificity of 0.88 (95% CI 0.83-0.91; 95% PI 0.62-0.97). Gradient boosting had the highest pooled AUROC (0.92), but CIs overlapped across algorithms. Externally validated models had a pooled AUROC of 0.85, lower than that of internal ones (0.91). The secondary analysis of all 115 models yielded consistent results. Meta‑regression identified no significant covariates. PROBAST assessment revealed that half of the studies were at high risk of bias. Conclusions: This review provides the first quantitative synthesis of ML‑based sarcopenia prediction models, with several innovations: (1) it provides algorithm‑stratified pooled estimates of diagnostic accuracy, (2) it formally quantifies performance across algorithms and addresses the unit‑of‑analysis issue through a 2‑tier approach, and (3) it quantifies the performance gap between externally and internally validated models. By identifying specific weaknesses—insufficient external validation, poor calibration reporting, and high risk of bias—this review offers a roadmap for improving future studies. Practically, these models may serve as cost‑effective prescreening tools. However, GRADE certainty was very low, with substantial heterogeneity, insufficient external validation, and high risk of bias, indicating that current models are not yet ready for routine deployment. Future research should prioritize rigorous external validation, transparent reporting, calibration assessment, and clinically implementable design. Clinical Trial: PROSPERO CRD420251267598; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420251267598
title: Predictive Modeling of Sarcopenia Using Machine Learning: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis

summary: Background: Digital nursing technologies (DNTs) have the potential to improve the quality and continuity of home care by supporting nurses, care recipients, and informal caregivers. Despite growing research on DNTs, the home care setting remains underrepresented, particularly regarding implementation strategies using an established implementation science framework. Therefore, this scoping review systematically maps implementation strategies for DNTs in home care using the Expert Recommendations for Implementing Change (ERIC) framework. Objective: We aimed to identify and map ERIC implementation strategies proposed or used for DNTs in home care. Additionally, we aimed to derive operationalized practical recommendations for decision-makers and implementation practitioners in nursing services. Methods: We conducted a scoping review with a systematic literature search in MEDLINE via PubMed, CINAHL via EBSCO, and Scopus via Elsevier in March 2025, with an updated search in July 2026. Guided by the PCC (Population, Concept, and Context) framework, we included primary studies and study protocols that addressed the implementation of a DNT in home care and were published between 2015 and 2026. We excluded studies from other health care settings, technologies not related to nursing, concept papers, and reviews. Data charting was conducted in MAXQDA 24 (VERBI Software) using deductive content analysis. We applied and operationalized the 73 ERIC implementation strategies to define our deductive category system. Results: A total of 22 articles with 18 distinct DNTs were included in this review. Most of them are implementation studies conducted in Europe and published in 2022. Most DNTs focused on home care using sensor-based monitoring and telehealth solutions for people with dementia, chronic conditions, or palliative care needs. Additional DNTs included mobile apps for symptom monitoring, decision-support systems, communication platforms, and a robotic medication management system. Deductive analysis based on the ERIC framework identified 48 of 73 implementation strategies across the included DNTs. The most frequently reported ERIC strategies were: conduct educational meetings (n=14), promote adaptability (n=14), conduct ongoing training (n=9), and train-the-trainer (n=9). The identified ERIC implementation strategies showed high heterogeneity across the included DNTs. Conclusions: These frequently reported ERIC implementation strategies may function as a multifaceted implementation strategy. However, they need to be empirically evaluated regarding their feasibility, appropriateness, and effectiveness for the implementation of DNTs in home care. In addition, researchers should ensure transparent reporting of implementation strategies by explicitly operationalizing them and applying established frameworks, such as the ERIC framework, to facilitate comparability across studies. Finally, practical guidance derived from ERIC implementation strategies should be specified in greater detail, including information on how, when, and for what duration individual implementation strategies should be applied. Trial Registration: OSF Registries osf.io/dsrh8; https://osf.io/dsrh8/overview
title: Implementation Strategies for Digital Nursing Technologies in Home Care: Scoping Review
